content.chiefComplaint: Severe burns following a house fire

nursesNotes.author: RN Trauma
nursesNotes.entry: Patient arrived via EMS intubated. Reports being trapped in burning structure for approx 20 mins. Deep partial and full-thickness burns noted to face, chest, abdomen, bilateral anterior arms, and anterior thighs. Singed nasal hairs and soot in oropharynx noted prior to intubation. 2 large bore IVs patent.

nursesNotes.author: RN Trauma
nursesNotes.entry: Foley catheter placed, drained 15 mL dark red urine. Peripheral pulses weak but palpable. Extremities cool. Parkland formula resuscitation initiated. Escharotomy kit at bedside due to circumferential chest burns.

historyPhysical.hpi: 42yo male rescued from residential fire. Prolonged extrication. Intubated on scene for airway protection due to stridor.

physicalExam.skin: 45% TBSA mixed burns. Chest eschar tight.
physicalExam.respiratory: Coarse breath sounds, soot in sputum

radiology.findings: ETT in good position. Diffuse patchy infiltrates suggesting inhalation injury. No pneumothorax.

rationale.caseSummary: A patient with 45% TBSA burns and inhalation injury presents in the emergent phase. The priority is fluid resuscitation to prevent hypovolemic shock and managing airway compromise.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Fluid shifts in major burns cause massive intravascular volume loss (hypovolemic shock). Hyperkalemia occurs from cell lysis. Hemoconcentration (high Hct) reflects volume loss. Myoglobinuria (red urine) risks renal failure.
rationale.trap: Assuming the high Hematocrit means the patient has 'too much blood' or is stable. It actually indicates severe dehydration/volume depletion (hemoconcentration).
rationale.goldenRule: In the first 24 hours of a major burn, the patient is hypovolemic, hyperkalemic, and hyponatremic.

steps.description: Signs of Burn Shock: Hypotension, Tachycardia, High Hct.
Calculate fluid needs (Parkland) and identify complications (Compartment syndrome).

difficulty.label: Evaluation
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Focus on the ABCs and Fluid status. Airway is secured, so Circulation (Fluids) is the next priority.

mnemonic.title: Emergent Phase Risks
mnemonic.content: 6 H's: Hypovolemia, Hyperkalemia, Hyponatremia, Hemoconcentration, Hypothermia, Hypoxia (Inhalation)
mnemonic.explanation: Key physiological derangements in the first 24-48 hours.

cheatSheet.title: Burn Resuscitation Pearls
points: Urine Output is the best indicator of resuscitation adequacy.
LR is the fluid of choice (buffers acidosis).

referenceInfo.anatomy: Capillary endothelial damage leads to leakage of plasma proteins into interstitial space.
referenceInfo.physiology: Massive fluid shift (third spacing) reduces cardiac output. Cell destruction releases Potassium. Muscle damage releases Myoglobin.
referenceInfo.pharm: Lactated Ringers is isotonic and metabolizes to bicarbonate, helping correct metabolic acidosis.

screens.prompt: Highlight the findings requiring immediate intervention.
screens.text: The patient has singed nasal hairs and soot in the oropharynx. Urine output is 15 mL of dark red urine. The chest burn eschar is circumferential and tight. Heart rate is 128 bpm. Temperature is 96.5°F. Potassium is 6.2 mEq/L. The patient has a history of hypertension.

rationale.caseSummary: Identifying critical complications of thermal injury: Airway, Renal, and Circulation.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Singed hairs/soot indicate inhalation injury (Airway). Dark red urine indicates myoglobinuria (Renal threat). Circumferential chest burns restrict breathing (Breathing/Circulation). Hyperkalemia (6.2) risks cardiac arrest. Tachycardia is expected compensatory. Hypothermia is a risk but less immediate than airway/K+.
rationale.trap: Prioritizing the temperature or expected tachycardia over the life-threatening potassium or airway signs.
rationale.goldenRule: Dark urine in burns = Myoglobinuria -> Rhabdomyolysis -> Renal Failure. Flush it out!

steps.description: Identify red flags: Airway soot, Red urine, Tight chest.
These threaten A, B, and Kidneys.

mnemonic.title: Burn Red Flags
mnemonic.content: Soot (Inhalation), Red Pee (Myoglobin), Tight Skin (Compartment), High K+ (Heart)

cheatSheet.title: Assessment Cues
points: Myoglobinuria -> Increase fluids to flush kidneys.

referenceInfo.anatomy: Myoglobin is a large protein that clogs renal tubules.
referenceInfo.physiology: Eschar is dead, inelastic tissue. If circumferential, it acts like a tourniquet or corset, preventing expansion.
referenceInfo.pharm: Sodium Bicarbonate may be used to alkalize urine and prevent myoglobin precipitation.

rationales.h1,: [Hook] Singed nasal hairs. [Breakdown] High suspicion for inhalation injury and potential airway edema. [Trap] Waiting for stridor to appear (too late).
rationales.h2,: [Hook] Soot in oropharynx. [Breakdown] Confirms smoke inhalation, risk of glottic edema and CO poisoning. [Trap] Assuming patent airway is stable.
rationales.h3,: [Hook] 15 mL dark red urine. [Breakdown] Oliguria + Myoglobinuria (Rhabdomyolysis) indicates acute tubular necrosis risk. [Trap] Thinking it's concentrated urine only.
rationales.h4,: [Hook] Circumferential/Tight eschar. [Breakdown] Restricts chest expansion, leading to respiratory failure (mechanical). [Trap] Confusing with normal edema.
rationales.h5,: [Hook] HR 128 bpm. [Breakdown] Expected compensatory response to shock/pain. Not the primary 'fixable' problem (fix fluids first). [Trap] Treating the rate with meds.
rationales.h6,: [Hook] Temp 96.5°F. [Breakdown] Mild hypothermia is common due to skin loss. Needs warming but not as urgent as Airway/K+. [Trap] Prioritizing comfort over ABCs.
rationales.h7,: [Hook] K+ 6.2 mEq/L. [Breakdown] Critical Hyperkalemia from cell lysis. Risk of arrhythmias. [Trap] Ignoring electrolyte shifts.
rationales.h8,: [Hook] History of HTN. [Breakdown] Chronic condition not relevant to acute resuscitation priorities. [Trap] Focusing on history.

screens.prompt: For each finding, indicate if it supports Hypovolemic Shock, Inhalation Injury, or Compartment Syndrome.

rows.rationale: Hemoconcentration due to loss of plasma volume.
Indicates Carbon Monoxide poisoning from smoke.

rationale.caseSummary: The patient is presenting with all three major complications.
rationale.answerAnalysis: High Hct/Lactate = Volume loss (Shock). CO/Stridor = Airway (Inhalation). Lost pulses/High pressures = Restriction (Compartment).
rationale.trap: Thinking high airway pressures are always ARDS/Lung injury. In burns, check the chest wall compliance (eschar) first.
rationale.goldenRule: High Hct in a trauma/burn patient means they are DRY (Hemoconcentrated), not that they have too much blood.

steps.description: Group signs by system: Circulatory (Shock), Respiratory (Inhalation), Mechanical (Compartment).

mnemonic.title: Burn Triad of Death
mnemonic.explanation: The three killers in the first 24 hours.

cheatSheet.title: Diagnostic Clues
points: Pain > Injury or Numbness = Compartment Syndrome.

referenceInfo.anatomy: Fascial compartments in extremities; Chest wall mechanics.
referenceInfo.physiology: CO binds Hgb 200x stronger than O2. Shock is distributive/hypovolemic.
referenceInfo.pharm: 100% O2 decreases CO half-life from 4 hours to 45 mins.

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Connect pathophysiology to lab values (Hemoconcentration = Hypovolemia).

screens.prompt: Drag the nursing actions into the correct priority order.

orderedOptions.text: Assess airway patency and endotracheal tube security
orderedOptions.rationale: Airway is always priority #1, especially with inhalation injury.

orderedOptions.text: Titrate Lactated Ringers to maintain urine output

orderedOptions.rationale: Comfort is important but follows ABCs.

rationale.answerAnalysis: Airway integrity is the absolute prerequisite. Fluid resuscitation treats the lethal shock state. Escharotomy is a procedure for a specific complication. Pain meds are supportive.
rationale.trap: Stopping resuscitation to do a procedure (escharotomy) before stabilizing the volume status, or prioritizing pain over shock.
rationale.goldenRule: You can't resuscitate a patient who can't breathe. Airway -> Fluids -> Procedures.

referenceInfo.anatomy: Glottis can swell shut in minutes.
referenceInfo.physiology: Hypovolemia leads to cardiac arrest if not treated aggressively.
referenceInfo.pharm: Opioids can cause hypotension; ensure fluids are running.

screens.prompt: Complete the diagram: Action, Condition, Parameters.

rationale.caseSummary: The patient has dark red urine (myoglobin) and low output. This is a specific renal threat.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Condition is Rhabdomyolysis/Myoglobinuria. Actions: FLUSH the kidneys. Increase fluids (higher target UOP 75-100mL/hr vs standard 30-50). Mannitol (osmotic diuretic) keeps tubules open. Bicarb alkalizes urine to prevent pigment precipitation. Escharotomy treats compartment syndrome, not directly the renal issue (though related).
rationale.trap: Treating with standard fluid goals (30mL/hr). In myoglobinuria, you must drive the kidneys harder to prevent clogging.
rationale.goldenRule: Red Urine = Double the Fluid Goal. Flush until clear.

mnemonic.title: Myoglobin Management
mnemonic.explanation: Three pillars of treating pigment nephropathy.

referenceInfo.physiology: Myoglobin precipitates in acidic urine, causing obstruction.
referenceInfo.pharm: Mannitol draws fluid into nephron; Bicarbonate raises pH.

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Identify the specific complication requiring altered fluid goals.

screens.text: The nurse anticipates administering %{d1} to treat %{d2}.

options.rationale: Insulin shifts Potassium into cells; Dextrose prevents hypoglycemia. Standard hyperkalemia cocktail.
Too slow for emergency treatment of K+ 6.2.

rationale.caseSummary: Cell lysis releases massive K+. Levels > 6.0 require shifting agents.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Insulin/D50 is the fastest temporary fix to shift K+ into cells to protect the heart. Kayexalate takes hours. Calcium gluconate (not listed) stabilizes the heart but doesn't lower K+.
rationale.trap: Ignoring the K+ because 'burns cause tissue damage'. K+ 6.2 can cause V-Fib regardless of the cause.
rationale.goldenRule: See High K+ -> Protect Heart (Calcium) -> Shift K+ (Insulin/Albuterol) -> Eliminate K+ (Lasix/Kayexalate).

mnemonic.title: C-BIG-K-Drop
mnemonic.content: C-alcium, B-icarb, I-nsulin, G-lucose, K-ayexalate, D-ialysis

referenceInfo.physiology: High K+ lowers resting membrane potential, making myocardium irritable.

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Prioritize immediate cardiac protection over long-term elimination.

screens.prompt: Which findings indicate the resuscitation is adequate? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Meets the higher goal for myoglobinuria (75-100 mL/hr).
Trending down suggests intravascular volume is replenishing.
Rising Hct indicates worsening dehydration/fluid loss.

rationale.caseSummary: Assessing if the fluids are working.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Adequate resuscitation is marked by: UOP meeting goal, MAP > 65, down-trending HR (resolving shock), and normalizing labs (Hct and Lactate should drop).
rationale.trap: Thinking a high Hct is good. In burns, we want the Hct to drop (dilution) back to normal.
rationale.goldenRule: Urine Output is the 'Vital Sign' of Burn Resuscitation.

referenceInfo.physiology: Adequate UOP proves the kidneys (and thus the core organs) are perfused.
referenceInfo.pharm: Parkland formula is just a starting point; titrate to the patient.

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Evaluate trends. Rising bad markers (Lactate/Hct) = Failure. Normalizing markers = Success.

historyPhysical.hpi: 34-year-old male presents with sharp, retrosternal chest pain that began 2 days ago. Pain radiates to the left trapezius ridge and worsens with inspiration and lying supine. He reports relief when sitting up and leaning forward. Patient had a 'flu-like illness' 2 weeks ago.

physicalExam.cardiovascular: Tachycardia, high-pitched scratching sound heard at LSB
physicalExam.respiratory: Lungs clear but shallow breath sounds due to pain

nursesNotes.author: RN Emergency
nursesNotes.entry: Patient triage: Complaints of sharp chest pain 8/10. States 'it feels like a knife when I breathe in.' Positioned sitting upright, leaning over bedside table. ECG obtained. Friction rub audible at left sternal border.

nursesNotes.author: RN Emergency
nursesNotes.entry: ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevation in precordial leads with PR depression. Troponin I negative. Patient remains tachypneic due to pleuritic pain. Vitals stable but febrile.

nursesNotes.author: RN Emergency
nursesNotes.entry: Dr. Cardio evaluated. Concern for inflammatory process vs ACS. Echocardiogram ordered to rule out effusion/tamponade. Pain management initiated.

radiology.finding: Normal cardiac silhouette. No pulmonary edema or consolidation.
radiology.impression: No acute cardiopulmonary process identified on plain film.

rationale.goldenRule: Distinguish Pericarditis from MI: Pericarditis pain changes with position/respiration and ECG changes are diffuse (everywhere), whereas MI pain is constant and ECG changes are localized to coronary territories.

mnemonic.title: FRICTION
mnemonic.content: F-Friction rub, R-Radiating pain to trap, I-Increased pain on inspiration, C-Chest pain (sharp), T-Trouble breathing (supine), I-Infection (viral hx), O-On leaning forward pain lessens, N-NSAIDs are first line
mnemonic.explanation: Summarizes the key assessment findings and management for Acute Pericarditis.

referenceInfo.anatomy: Acute Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardial sac, often viral or idiopathic. The classic presentation includes pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward, a pericardial friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression on ECG.
referenceInfo.physiology: Inflammation of the pericardium causes the layers to rub against each other (friction rub) and irritate local nerves (pain). The ECG changes reflect superficial myocardial inflammation (ST elevation) and atrial injury (PR depression). Effusions may develop if fluid accumulates rapidly.

rationale.pathophysiology: Inflammation of the pericardium causes the layers to rub against each other (friction rub) and irritate local nerves (pain). The ECG changes reflect superficial myocardial inflammation (ST elevation) and atrial injury (PR depression). Effusions may develop if fluid accumulates rapidly.
rationale.general: Acute Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardial sac, often viral or idiopathic. The classic presentation includes pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward, a pericardial friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression on ECG.
rationale.safetyCheck: CRITICAL: Monitor for signs of Cardiac Tamponade (Beck's Triad: Hypotension, JVD, Muffled Heart Sounds). This is a life-threatening complication where fluid compresses the heart, preventing filling.
rationale.clinicalTakeaway: Distinguish Pericarditis from MI: Pericarditis pain changes with position/respiration and ECG changes are diffuse (everywhere), whereas MI pain is constant and ECG changes are localized to coronary territories.

physicalExam.general: Diaphoretic, using accessory muscles to breathe
physicalExam.cardiovascular: S3 gallop noted, JVD distended to mandible
physicalExam.respiratory: Coarse crackles auscultated up to apices bilaterally

nursesNotes.author: RN Triage
nursesNotes.entry: Patient arrived via private vehicle. Visible respiratory distress. SpO2 86% on RA. Placed on 15L NRB. BP 178/94. Pink frothy sputum noted. Immediate transfer to Resus bay.

nursesNotes.author: RN Primary
nursesNotes.entry: IV access established #18g LAC. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Patient struggling to speak in full sentences. Breath sounds wet throughout. Dr. Cardio at bedside.

nursesNotes.author: RN Primary
nursesNotes.entry: Foley catheter inserted. Output 20mL concentrated urine. Patient anxious, diaphoretic. BP remains elevated.

radiology.finding: Significant cardiomegaly. Diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates with Kerley B lines ('Batwing appearance').
radiology.impression: Severe Pulmonary Edema consistent with CHF exacerbation.

referenceInfo.anatomy: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure (ADHF) presenting as Flash Pulmonary Edema. The left ventricle fails to pump effectively, causing blood to back up into the pulmonary vasculature, leading to fluid extravasation into alveoli (pink frothy sputum).
referenceInfo.physiology: Increased afterload (HTN) + Volume overload (missed diuretics) -> Elevated Left Ventricular End Diastolic Pressure (LVEDP) -> Increased Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure -> Fluid crosses capillary membrane into alveoli -> Hypoxia -> Sympathetic surge -> Tachycardia/Vasoconstriction -> Worsening Cycle.
